name: The Kármán Line
statement: The conventional edge of space sits about a hundred kilometres up, where wings stop working.
statementAccent: about a hundred kilometres up, where wings stop working
meaning: The Kármán line is a conventional definition of the boundary between Earth's atmosphere and outer space, most commonly set at an altitude of one hundred kilometres, about sixty-two miles, above mean sea level. It is a widely but not universally accepted marker of where space begins, adopted for record-keeping and the awarding of astronaut status. The line has no sharp physical meaning, since the atmosphere thins gradually rather than ending abruptly, but it captures a real transition: above roughly this height, the air is too thin for aircraft to fly aerodynamically, and travel must instead rely on orbital motion. The line is named after the Hungarian-American engineer and physicist Theodore von Kármán, who reasoned about the altitude at which aeronautics gives way to astronautics. Its exact value is a matter of convention and some dispute: the international governing body for aeronautics uses one hundred kilometres, while the United States has often used about eighty kilometres, or fifty miles, instead.
mechanism: Von Kármán's reasoning rested on how an aircraft stays aloft. A conventional aircraft generates lift by moving through the air, and the thinner the air, the faster it must fly to produce enough lift to support its weight. As altitude increases and the atmosphere thins, the speed required for aerodynamic flight climbs, until at a certain height the aircraft would need to travel faster than orbital velocity, the speed at which it would simply orbit, to get enough lift. Above that altitude, aerodynamic flight is no longer possible and only orbital motion, astronautics, will keep a vehicle up, so von Kármán identified this as a natural boundary where aeronautics ends and astronautics begins. His original calculation put the figure at around eighty-four kilometres, and the round number of one hundred kilometres was later adopted as a convenient convention by the international aeronautics federation. The line is thus a physically motivated but conventional boundary, marking a transition in how flight works rather than a hard edge to the atmosphere.

examples.text: Above the Kármán line the air is too thin for wings to generate lift at any reasonable speed, so only orbital motion keeps a vehicle aloft.
The international aeronautics federation uses the hundred-kilometre Kármán line to mark spaceflight and the boundary for astronautics.
The United States has often used about eighty kilometres, or fifty miles, as its threshold for awarding astronaut wings, differing from the Kármán line.

variants.name: The FAI 100 km convention
variants.text: The Fédération Aéronautique Internationale's use of one hundred kilometres as the boundary of space for records and astronautics.

variants.name: The US 80 km threshold
variants.text: The roughly eighty-kilometre, or fifty-mile, altitude used by parts of the United States as its boundary for awarding astronaut status.

whyItMatters: The Kármán line matters because defining where space begins has practical consequences for law, records, and the recognition of astronauts, even though the atmosphere has no true edge. As a widely used convention, the hundred-kilometre line determines whether a flight counts as spaceflight for international records and who is credited as having reached space, and it figures in discussions of airspace sovereignty and the legal regime governing space versus air. Its physical basis, von Kármán's insight that aerodynamic flight becomes impossible where the air is too thin, gives the line a rationale grounded in real physics, illustrating the genuine transition from aeronautics to astronautics. At the same time, the dispute between the hundred-kilometre and eighty-kilometre definitions highlights that the boundary is a human choice, not a fact of nature, with real stakes for who earns astronaut status. The Kármán line thus sits at the intersection of physics, engineering, law, and record-keeping, a useful and much-cited marker of the threshold of space.

limits: The Kármán line is a convention, not a sharp physical boundary, since the atmosphere fades out gradually and there is no altitude at which space abruptly begins. Its value is disputed: the international aeronautics federation uses one hundred kilometres, while the United States and some analyses use about eighty kilometres, or fifty miles, and von Kármán's own calculation gave a figure closer to eighty-four kilometres, so the round hundred-kilometre number is a chosen standard rather than a derived constant. The precise altitude at which aerodynamic flight fails also depends on the vehicle and conditions. So the Kármán line is a useful and widely adopted marker of the edge of space, best understood as a physically motivated convention whose exact value is a matter of definition and ongoing debate rather than a fixed natural fact.
misreadings: The Kármán line is not a real physical edge where the atmosphere stops; the air thins gradually, and the line is a chosen convention. Its value is not universally agreed, since the international federation uses one hundred kilometres while the United States often uses about eighty, so which flights count as spaceflight can differ. And von Kármán's own figure was nearer eighty-four kilometres, with one hundred a rounded standard, so treating the line as a hard boundary of the atmosphere, or as a single undisputed altitude, misreads a physically motivated but conventional marker of where space is said to begin.
origin: Named after the Hungarian-American engineer and physicist Theodore von Kármán, who reasoned about the altitude where aerodynamic flight fails; conventionally set at 100 km by the Fédération Aéronautique Internationale.
